this was my little town of marshall over the weekend - under 15 feet of water. anything you can do to help us in western north carolina would be greatly appreciated. and most of all, please pray for us!i'm grateful to say my home and immediate family are safe, but a lot of my friends lost their homes and businesses, and even more of us will suffer as we feel the economic toll of the catastrophe.marshall was particularly hard-hit because it was downriver from a plastics plant, so the mud that was deposited is toxic.   today i want to show you someplace really special, and not a lot of people know about it, because it's way up high on a remote backwoods mountaintop.it's a little country church that was built before electricity came here, and it's still not hooked up to the utilities.and it's a tiny, sweet little building built by the locals from cinderblock in the 1950s, way back in a quiet clearing. when you park your car and turn the engine off, you won't hear anything but the little chirpy birds in the trees.it's very restful here.when i first visited this place ten or fifteen years ago, it was almost empty and very beautiful in its bare simplicity.since then, the community has brought it back into use, and it has a new kind of beauty: the beauty of a homely little place that somebody cares about.they put in some old-fashioned oil lamps, and a woodstove, and a few rows of comfortable pews with soft pink cushions.there's no fancy light show at this altar, no loud sound system, no big band with electric guitars. there's not even a piano like you'll find in the other little churches around here.but there's a stack of old worn-out hymnals, and the acoustics in this little one-room church are pretty good.what hymns would you sing here? chemical reactivity and fire risk. establishing a nationwide infrastructure for safe handling is costly and complex, especially in rural areas.  economic barriers: recycling lithium batteries is expensive compared to landfilling or producing new batteries. low commodity prices for recycled materials (e.g., lithium, cobalt) and high processing costs deter investment in large-scale recycling facilities.  limited public awareness: many consumers are unaware of proper disposal methods or lack convenient access to recycling drop-off points, reducing participation rates and complicating efforts to scale programs nationally.  technological limitations: current recycling technologies, like pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy, are energy-intensive and recover only a fraction of materials. emerging methods (e.g., direct recycling) are not yet commercially scalable, hindering efficient nationwide systems.  safety concerns: lithium batteries pose fire and explosion risks during collection, transport, and processing. developing standardized safety protocols across a national program requires significant coordination and investment.  industry responsibility: while some manufacturers support recycling, there s no universal producer responsibility mandate in the u.s. unlike the eu, where battery producers must finance recycling, u.s. companies face less pressure to should be so situated as to be able to exercise free power of choice, without the intervention of any element of force, fraud, deceit, duress, overreaching, or other ulterior form of constraint or coercion; and should have sufficient knowledge and comprehension of the elements of the subject matter involved as to enable him to make an understanding and enlightened decision. this latter element requires that before the acceptance of an affirmative decision by the experimental subject there should be made known to him the nature, duration, and purpose of the experiment; the method and means by which it is to be conducted; all inconveniences and hazards reasonably to be expected; and the effects upon his health or person which may possibly come from his participation in the experiment.the duty and responsibility for ascertaining the quality of the consent rests upon each individual who initiates, directs, or engages in the experiment. it is a personal duty and responsibility which may not be delegated to another with impunity. 2. the experiment should be such as to yield fruitful results for the good of society, unprocurable by other methods or means of study, and not random and unnecessary in nature. 3. the experiment should be so designed and based on the results of animal experimentation and a knowledge of the natural history of the disease or other problem under study that the anticipated results justify the performance of the experiment. 4. the experiment should be so conducted as to avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering and injury. 5. no experiment should be conducted where there is an a priori reason to believe that death or disabling injury will occur;
